title: Routine antenatal care (uncomplicated pregnancy)
subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
summary: WHO recommends at least 8 antenatal contacts. Book by 10 weeks (NICE), give folic acid, iron and (where intake is low) calcium, screen for anaemia, infections, blood group, bacteriuria and gestational diabetes risk, scan before 24 weeks, give aspirin 75 to 150 mg from 12 weeks if at pre-eclampsia risk, and refer promptly for red flags.

sections.title: Schedule and booking contact
items: WHO 2016: at least 8 contacts, the first by 12 weeks, then at 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks (return at 41 weeks if not delivered).
NICE NG201: booking with a midwife by 10+0 weeks (within 2 weeks if referred after 9+0 weeks); plan 10 routine appointments for nulliparous and 7 for parous women.

At booking: medical, obstetric, mental health and social history (including domestic abuse), height, weight and BMI, BP and urine dipstick; assess risks of pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, VTE and fetal growth restriction.
Ask about tobacco, second-hand smoke, alcohol and other substances at booking and at every contact; refer smokers for cessation support.

sections.title: Screening tests
items: Booking bloods: FBC, blood group, RhD status and red cell antibodies; HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B; sickle cell and thalassaemia screening per local programme. Repeat FBC and antibodies at 28 weeks (NICE).
Anaemia (WHO 2024): Hb below 11.0 g/dL in the first and third trimesters, below 10.5 g/dL in the second. Use FBC, or a haemoglobinometer where FBC is unavailable.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: midstream urine culture (Gram stain if culture is unavailable; not dipstick). Treat a positive result with a 7-day antibiotic course (WHO).

Ultrasound: WHO recommends one scan before 24 weeks. NICE: dating scan at 11+2 to 14+1 weeks (gestation, multiple pregnancy, combined aneuploidy screening if chosen) and anomaly scan at 18+0 to 20+6 weeks (anomalies, placental site).
Gestational diabetes: NICE offers a 75 g OGTT at 24+0 to 28+0 weeks to women with risk factors (NICE NG3); WHO classifies hyperglycaemia first found in pregnancy by WHO 2013 criteria.
Where TB prevalence is 100 per 100,000 or more, screen systematically for active TB (WHO).

sections.title: Supplements and prevention
items: Folic acid 400 micrograms daily from before conception to 12 weeks. Use 5 mg daily if at higher neural tube defect risk: previous or family history of NTD, type 1 or 2 diabetes, sickle cell disease or thalassaemia, antiepileptic or antiretroviral drugs (NICE 2025; raised BMI alone is not an indication).

Iron: WHO recommends daily oral iron 30 to 60 mg elemental iron with 400 micrograms folic acid throughout pregnancy (weekly 120 mg iron with 2.8 mg folic acid if daily dosing is not tolerated and anaemia prevalence is under 20%).
Calcium 1.5 to 2.0 g elemental calcium daily where dietary calcium intake is low, to reduce pre-eclampsia (WHO).

Aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth for any 1 high-risk factor: hypertensive disease in a previous pregnancy, chronic kidney disease, SLE or antiphospholipid syndrome, type 1 or 2 diabetes, chronic hypertension (NICE NG133).
Aspirin also for more than 1 moderate factor: nulliparity, age 40 or over, pregnancy interval over 10 years, BMI 35 kg/m2 or more at booking, family history of pre-eclampsia, multifetal pregnancy.
Vitamin D 10 micrograms (400 IU) daily: NICE advises it October to March, and all year with darker skin or little sun exposure; WHO does not recommend routine vitamin D.
Vaccines: tetanus toxoid according to previous vaccination (WHO); influenza, pertussis and RSV vaccines per the national schedule.
Anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks for non-sensitised RhD-negative women (NICE); WHO recommends routine antenatal anti-D only within research.

sections.title: At every contact
items: Blood pressure with a device validated for pregnancy, and urine dipstick for protein, at every routine appointment (NICE).

Symphysis-fundal height at each appointment after 24+0 weeks (not more often than every 2 weeks), plotted on a growth chart. Offer a scan if small for dates; consider one if large. No routine scans after 28 weeks in uncomplicated singleton pregnancy.
From 24+0 weeks ask about fetal movements at each contact and advise her to report reduced movements immediately, day or night.
Abdominal palpation for presentation from 36+0 weeks; confirm suspected breech by ultrasound and offer external cephalic version.
Reassess pre-eclampsia and fetal growth risk in the second trimester. Advise healthy eating, activity, caffeine under 300 mg a day, no alcohol or smoking, and sleeping on her side after 28 weeks.

sections.title: When to refer
items: New BP 140/90 mmHg or higher after 20+0 weeks: secondary care review within 24 hours. BP 160/110 mmHg or higher: same-day review.

Pre-eclampsia symptoms (severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, sudden swelling), vaginal bleeding after 13 weeks, reduced fetal movements, abdominal pain, fever, ruptured membranes or preterm contractions: same-day obstetric assessment.
Vaginal bleeding after 13 weeks in an RhD-negative woman at risk of isoimmunisation: give anti-D.
Severe vomiting not responding to outpatient treatment (hyperemesis gravidarum): consider admission.

Pre-existing disease (diabetes, hypertension, epilepsy, heart or kidney disease, HIV), previous serious complications, abnormal screening results or VTE risk factors: obstetrician-led care per local pathway.

sections.title: Setting-specific measures
items: Malaria-endemic Africa: intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine from the second trimester, doses at least 1 month apart, aiming for 3 or more doses (WHO).
Endemic helminth areas: preventive anthelminthic after the first trimester (WHO).
High HIV prevalence: provider-initiated HIV testing and offer oral PrEP containing tenofovir disoproxil to women at substantial risk (WHO).

India (MoHFW) differs: IFA with 60 mg elemental iron and 500 micrograms folic acid daily from the second trimester for at least 180 days, albendazole 400 mg after the first trimester, and universal GDM testing with a 75 g glucose load (see the India anaemia and GDM protocols).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Using urine dipstick instead of culture to screen for asymptomatic bacteriuria.
Missing women who qualify for aspirin, or starting it late; start from 12 weeks.
Skipping BP and urine checks at routine contacts and missing new hypertension after 20 weeks.
Routine antenatal CTG or Doppler in low-risk pregnancy (WHO does not recommend them).

drugs.name: Folic acid
drugs.dose: 400 micrograms orally daily from preconception to 12 weeks; 5 mg daily if at increased NTD risk

drugs.name: Iron with folic acid (WHO)
drugs.dose: 30 to 60 mg elemental iron plus 400 micrograms folic acid orally daily throughout pregnancy
drugs.notes: Weekly 120 mg iron with 2.8 mg folic acid if daily dosing is not tolerated and anaemia prevalence is under 20%.

drugs.name: Calcium
drugs.dose: 1.5 to 2.0 g elemental calcium orally daily in divided doses
drugs.notes: Where dietary calcium intake is low. Take at a different time from iron.

drugs.name: Aspirin (pre-eclampsia prevention)
drugs.dose: 75 to 150 mg orally once daily from 12 weeks until birth
drugs.notes: 1 high-risk factor or more than 1 moderate risk factor (NICE NG133).

drugs.name: Vitamin D
drugs.notes: NICE advice; WHO does not recommend routine supplementation.

drugs.name: Anti-D immunoglobulin
drugs.dose: IM at 28 weeks (single-dose regimen) or at 28 and 34 weeks (two-dose regimen), dose per product
drugs.notes: Non-sensitised RhD-negative women; also after sensitising events such as bleeding after 13 weeks.
